In the Plan we’ve highlighted 10 priorities that New Zealand needs to focus on over the next decade. 
 
One of these priorities is to complete catch-up on renewals in the water sector and restore affordability – sector affordability can be restored through national guidance on demand management, resourcing the economic regulator and providing assurance over investment proposals. 
 
What’s the problem?

💧New Zealanders use more water and invest more in water-related infrastructure than almost any other high-income country. 
📈 Councils plan to spend close to $50 billion over the next decade on renewing and expanding water networks. 
💵 As a result, household bills are expected to double in some instances. 
📪 Sustaining current high levels of investment will be unaffordable for some communities. 
🏠 From mid-1970s to mid-1990s we spent less on water than the rate of depreciation – our pipes and treatment plants have worn out faster than we replaced them. 
🚿 Councils are now dealing with a legacy of broken pipes, sewage 
overflows and leaks, as well as a need to invest to meet quality standards set by Taumata Arowai. 
 
So, what do we need to do?

⚙️ Encourage councils and water services providers to consider installing water meters and adopting volumetric pricing. 
🏛️ Ensure regulatory coordination – the Commerce Commission, the Water Services Authority – Taumata Arowai and regional councils will need to work together.
 
Find out more here: https://lnkd.in/eG4r5-Sy

Today we have published research, completed by Earth Sciences New Zealand and commissioned by Te Waihanga, showing that flood damage is expected to increase over the coming decades, with the impacts felt unevenly across the country. Flood-related financial losses are likely to exceed those from any other natural hazard.

Financial losses to infrastructure rise significantly under any modelled climate scenario. Under a scenario with high greenhouse gas emissions, the annual cost of inland flood damage to New Zealand’s infrastructure – our roads, our powerlines and other critical services – is estimated to increase from $300 million per year in 2025 to around $465 million in 2075. Coastal flooding damages are expected to almost double: from $165 million per year in 2025 to around $325 million in 2075.

Some regions, like Hawke’s Bay and Manawatū-Whanganui, face high expected losses relative to the overall size of their infrastructure networks – around double the national average. Regions such as Auckland, Wellington, and Taranaki tend to face lower losses proportionate to infrastructure exposed.

Read the research: https://lnkd.in/eAj8Mqw7

📸| Flooding of the river in Edgecumbe on April 6, 2017. Photo courtesy of NZFloodPics.

#NZ #Infrastructure #AssetManagement #TeWaihanga","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tewaihanga_nz-infrastructure-assetmanagement-activity-7478296562419466240-4L0b"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"New Zealand Infrastructure Commission, Te Waihanga","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/tewaihanga"},"datePublished":"2026-06-23T21:56:08.691Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tewaihanga_infrastructure-congestioncharging-priority-activity-7475305722507988992-RiJP","text":"💡 PRIORITY SPOTLIGHT | In February, we published our National Infrastructure Plan. In the Plan we highlighted 10 priorities that New Zealand needs to focus on over the next decade.
 
One of these priorities is to implement time-of-use charging and fleetwide road user charges – this is essential for improving the efficiency of our urban road networks, particularly in congested cities. 
 
What’s the problem?
 
🌆 Congestion in fast-growing cities is worsening. 
🛠️ Adding new capacity to existing roads is increasingly difficult and expensive. 
🚗 Congestion imposes productivity and wellbeing costs, with Auckland commuters losing 66 hours a year stuck in traffic and social and economic costs are estimated to reach $2.6 billion by 2026. 
🏢 If left unchecked, rising congestion will make cities less attractive, costlier, and less productive. 
 
So, what do we need to do?
 
⌚ Implement time-of-use charging in Auckland – enabling legislation exists but central and local government support is critical for designing and implementing. 
📍 Partner with local government. Congestion pressures are concentrated in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Tauranga, and Queenstown. Joint design, timing, and supporting investments will help ensure schemes are effective and publicly sustainable. 
⚙️ Integrate pricing into investment decisions. Congestion charging will change travel patterns and the timing of future investment needs. Business cases should explicitly account for these effects to ensure the right investments are made at the right time. 
🤝 Support the transition to universal road user charges. Modernising the largely paper-based system and expanding it to 3.5 million vehicles will be complex, but it can make transport funding fairer and more transparent. 
 
Find out more about our 10 infrastructure priorities for the decade ahead and read the Plan: https://lnkd.in/eG4r5-Sy

The IPP was set up as a process for central and local government, private organisations, and individuals to submit proposals that were assessed independently against clear and consistent criteria.

We started accepting voluntary applications to the IPP in 2024. Since it launched, the Commission has received nearly 150 proposals that were submitted voluntarily to the scheme. A total of 47 proposals were endorsed as infrastructure priorities. There are five newly endorsed proposals in round three.

Applications to the IPP are no longer being accepted while the Commission and the Treasury develop a new process for infrastructure investment assurance for central government infrastructure projects.

Find out more about the IPP and the changes to the investment assurance system: https://lnkd.in/eddSP-yT

This marks a new phase for New Zealand’s infrastructure system.

When we published the Plan earlier this year, we said New Zealand needed to do things differently to deliver the infrastructure we need to thrive over the next 30 years.

The Government’s response today, accepting the case for change and confirming the direction of reform, is a step in the right direction in improving performance and getting better value for money from our infrastructure.
The response formally addresses each of the 16 recommendations and 10 priority areas in the Plan. Thirteen of the 16 recommendations are fully supported and the remaining three supported in principle. Action on some of the recommendations is already underway.

Work with the Treasury is being undertaken to build a new assurance process for central government infrastructure investment. This will be in place on 1 November.

Find out more about the Government’s response to the Plan: https://lnkd.in/dxcYDJXP

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">💡PRIORITY SPOTLIGHT | In February we published our National Infrastructure Plan. In the Plan we’ve highlighted 10 priorities that New Zealand needs to focus on over the next decade. 
 
One of these priorities is to complete catch-up on renewals in the water sector and restore affordability – sector affordability can be restored through national guidance on demand management, resourcing the economic regulator and providing assurance over investment proposals. 
 
What’s the problem?

💧New Zealanders use more water and invest more in water-related infrastructure than almost any other high-income country. 
📈 Councils plan to spend close to $50 billion over the next decade on renewing and expanding water networks. 
💵 As a result, household bills are expected to double in some instances. 
📪 Sustaining current high levels of investment will be unaffordable for some communities. 
🏠 From mid-1970s to mid-1990s we spent less on water than the rate of depreciation – our pipes and treatment plants have worn out faster than we replaced them. 
🚿 Councils are now dealing with a legacy of broken pipes, sewage 
overflows and leaks, as well as a need to invest to meet quality standards set by Taumata Arowai. 
 
So, what do we need to do?

⚙️ Encourage councils and water services providers to consider installing water meters and adopting volumetric pricing. 
🏛️ Ensure regulatory coordination – the Commerce Commission, the Water Services Authority – Taumata Arowai and regional councils will need to work together.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">💡| How do different climate scenarios impact the expected damage to our infrastructure across New Zealand?

Today we have published research, completed by <a class="link" href="https://www.linkedin.com/company/earthsciencesnz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Earth Sciences New Zealand</a> and commissioned by Te Waihanga, showing that flood damage is expected to increase over the coming decades, with the impacts felt unevenly across the country. Flood-related financial losses are likely to exceed those from any other natural hazard.

Financial losses to infrastructure rise significantly under any modelled climate scenario. Under a scenario with high greenhouse gas emissions, the annual cost of inland flood damage to New Zealand’s infrastructure – our roads, our powerlines and other critical services – is estimated to increase from $300 million per year in 2025 to around $465 million in 2075. Coastal flooding damages are expected to almost double: from $165 million per year in 2025 to around $325 million in 2075.

Some regions, like Hawke’s Bay and Manawatū-Whanganui, face high expected losses relative to the overall size of their infrastructure networks – around double the national average. Regions such as Auckland, Wellington, and Taranaki tend to face lower losses proportionate to infrastructure exposed.

Read the research: <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/eAj8Mqw7?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/eAj8Mqw7</a>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">💡 PRIORITY SPOTLIGHT | In February, we published our National Infrastructure Plan. In the Plan we highlighted 10 priorities that New Zealand needs to focus on over the next decade.
 
One of these priorities is to implement time-of-use charging and fleetwide road user charges – this is essential for improving the efficiency of our urban road networks, particularly in congested cities. 
 
What’s the problem?
 
🌆 Congestion in fast-growing cities is worsening. 
🛠️ Adding new capacity to existing roads is increasingly difficult and expensive. 
🚗 Congestion imposes productivity and wellbeing costs, with Auckland commuters losing 66 hours a year stuck in traffic and social and economic costs are estimated to reach $2.6 billion by 2026. 
🏢 If left unchecked, rising congestion will make cities less attractive, costlier, and less productive. 
 
So, what do we need to do?
 
⌚ Implement time-of-use charging in Auckland – enabling legislation exists but central and local government support is critical for designing and implementing. 
📍 Partner with local government. Congestion pressures are concentrated in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Tauranga, and Queenstown. Joint design, timing, and supporting investments will help ensure schemes are effective and publicly sustainable. 
⚙️ Integrate pricing into investment decisions. Congestion charging will change travel patterns and the timing of future investment needs. Business cases should explicitly account for these effects to ensure the right investments are made at the right time. 
🤝 Support the transition to universal road user charges. Modernising the largely paper-based system and expanding it to 3.5 million vehicles will be complex, but it can make transport funding fairer and more transparent. 
 
Find out more about our 10 infrastructure priorities for the decade ahead and read the Plan: <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/eG4r5-Sy?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/eG4r5-Sy</a>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today, the Government has released its formal response to the National Infrastructure Plan. This marks a new phase for New Zealand’s infrastructure system.

When we published the Plan earlier this year, we said New Zealand needed to do things differently to deliver the infrastructure we need to thrive over the next 30 years.

The Government’s response today, accepting the case for change and confirming the direction of reform, is a step in the right direction in improving performance and getting better value for money from our infrastructure.
The response formally addresses each of the 16 recommendations and 10 priority areas in the Plan. Thirteen of the 16 recommendations are fully supported and the remaining three supported in principle. Action on some of the recommendations is already underway.

Work with the Treasury is being undertaken to build a new assurance process for central government infrastructure investment. This will be in place on 1 November.
